analysis.one_liner: Bans group health plans from imposing lifetime benefit caps below $5 million to $10 million.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban low lifetime caps on health benefits never got a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped group health plans and their insurers from capping total lifetime benefits below $5 million for the first three years and $10 million after that. That matters for people with cancer, organ transplants, or other catastrophic illnesses who can exhaust a low cap and lose coverage mid-treatment. Plans at employers with fewer than 20 employees were exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families in employer group plans facing catastrophic illness: a higher lifetime cap means their insurance cannot run out mid-treatment, protecting them from medical bankruptcy. Roughly the group market, including self-insured employer plans, is covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees with catastrophic illnesses in group plans

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and their insurers from imposing aggregate lifetime benefit limits below $5 million for the first three plan years after enactment and below $10 million thereafter.
Applies both to ERISA plans and to health insurance coverage in the group market, so workers covered under employer plans and under group insurance both get the protection.
Takes effect for plan years beginning two years after enactment, giving plans time to adjust.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer plans would absorb the cost of catastrophic claims that a low lifetime cap would otherwise have cut off, likely through somewhat higher premiums. Small employers (fewer than 20 employees) are exempt from the requirement.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to employers with 20 or more employees, so workers at small firms — where coverage is often weakest — get no protection.
Higher insurer costs for catastrophic claims would likely be passed into premiums for all group plan members, a real cost even if modest on average.
A very high floor still allows some lifetime cap; it limits but does not eliminate the risk of exhausting coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large for the relatively few families facing million-dollar illnesses — protection from losing coverage mid-treatment and medical bankruptcy — and the cost is a modest premium spread across all group plan members. The main design weakness is the carve-out for small employers, which leaves many vulnerable workers uncovered. On balance a well-targeted consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to their health and employer subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on June 5, 1997, with Reps. McDermott, Schumer, Miller of California, Tierney, and Weygand as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day of introduction.
Within three weeks it was sent to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action was taken: no markup, no floor vote, and the 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999 with the bill still in committee.
Thirty-two members cosponsored the bill — 30 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employer plans were better off because the bill died: they kept the freedom to impose low lifetime caps and cut off catastrophic claims. Patients with expensive chronic or catastrophic conditions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and large employer plans

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; never acted
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health and Environment Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or floor action during the 105th Congress.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Second committee of referral; never acted
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 30 of 32 cosponsors — with only 2 Republicans, and the bill died in committees controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers in the group market to keep paying catastrophic claims up to $5-10 million instead of cutting members off at a low lifetime cap. Insurers opposed such mandates, and the bill's death preserved their ability to limit exposure — at the cost of coverage for the sickest patients.

industries.industry: Large employers (20+ employees) sponsoring health plans
industries.note: Self-insured and insured employer plans would bear higher catastrophic claim costs, likely passed into premiums. Employers with fewer than 20 employees were exempt entirely.
